title: The Secret Lives of Japanese Temple Frogs
gist: Kyoto University environmental scientists surveyed frog populations across 31 Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines in Kyoto's Higashiyama district, finding that these urban water features function as significant amphibian habitats.

insights.claim: A Kyoto University research team surveyed frog populations at 31 temples, shrines, and adjacent water features in Kyoto's Higashiyama region, using visual identification, environmental DNA sampling, and acoustic recording of frog calls.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Documents a specific urban-ecology research methodology combining eDNA and bioacoustics for amphibian surveys.
insights.quote: The team focused on 31 temples, shrines, and adjacent areas in Kyoto's Higashiyama region, surveying their various ponds and streams for signs of frogs.

insights.claim: A study published in Urban Ecosystems concludes that Kyoto's hundreds of Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines function as urban amphibian hot spots due to their water features, making them both culturally and ecologically significant.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Frames religious/heritage sites as an overlooked category of urban green/blue infrastructure relevant to biodiversity conservation planning.
insights.quote: frogs in particular are drawn to their many water features, making the landmarks both culturally and ecologically important

insights.claim: Researchers also recorded characteristics of each water feature surveyed, including whether it was a pond or stream, presence or absence of koi, and vegetation type, to assess drivers of frog habitat suitability.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Identifies specific environmental variables (koi presence, vegetation) likely tested as predictors of amphibian presence.
insights.quote: They also collected data on the characteristics of the water features (ponds versus streams, the presence or absence of koi, types of vegetation, and so on).
